title: Inkitt tested its first app with $20 a day in ads, and it now makes around $130M a year
summary: Ali Albazaz kept hearing nobody would leave Kindle, but selling on Amazon had given Inkitt a 100% churn rate.
body_markdown:
Ali Albazaz, founder and CEO of Inkitt, started out selling ebooks on Amazon. Revenue jumped to "ten, 20, 30, $40,000 in monthly revenue on Amazon. And then we started to stagnate." When he looked for the reason, he found it in the metric every subscription operator watches: "What is our, you know, churn rate. And we're like, yeah, a 100% churn rate. Why? Because Amazon owns that whole relationship." Amazon kept the customer's email address and paid Inkitt at the end of the month, so there was no way to sell a reader the next part of a book.


Building a reading app was the fix, and people told him it was a strange one. "Do you think you can compete with Kindle?" they asked. "Why would people come to you? There is no reason."


The first version was built to find out. "We really quickly basically built an app that had like a slideshow for pictures," Ali says, filled with screenshots of text, and shipped it "within, I don't know, 3 or 4 days or so." Inkitt tested it with about $20 a day in ads. "And then we were like, whoa, you know, somebody now came and spent $10." About a year later, he says, "the app was making almost like $1 million a month." That app is Galatea, and Inkitt has sold direct in every business it has built since.


## **Ali says Inkitt hasn't had a single flop**


David Barnard assumed a content business must have plenty of flops. Ali disagreed: that is true of every company in entertainment, he said, "probably, except us. And we haven't had a single flop."


The claim rests on where the bets are placed. More than 2 million stories have been written on Inkitt's free platform, and the company watches how readers behave with them, not what they say in reviews, ratings or comments. "Are they finishing the book? Are they staying up all night to finish reading a book? Do they share that story with their friend?" Only stories that pass move to Galatea. Of those, Ali says, hedging as he goes, around 45% have made at least $100,000 in sales and about 16% have made over $1M, which he puts at 40 to 60 times the average publisher. David's reading is that the flops do happen, but on the free platform, where they cost Inkitt nothing.


## **30 A/B tests a month and 3,000 new ads a week**


Asked what other apps could borrow, Ali started with volume. Inkitt runs about 30 significant product tests a month: new subscription lengths, paywall positions, pricing, and whether the paywall appears on first open or after the user hits the aha moment. On the marketing side it tests about 3,000 new ad creatives a week. "There is nothing like a bad idea. You just need to test it."


The same goes for the stories. On Galatea, Inkitt rewrites openings and cliffhangers and measures which version sells the next chapter, hundreds of times a month. One investor joked that when Inkitt builds its theme park it will A/B test the roller coasters to see which makes people scream more. Ali's reply: "Yeah, that sounds like us."


## **CandyJar started with one product manager, one engineer, and 30 days**


In 2023 a colleague showed Ali ads for a microdrama app whose stories looked a lot like Galatea's. He put one product manager and one engineer on it and told them, "you have 30 days to build an app." Inkitt made two productions, at about $100,000 each, from books that had already earned $1M. The paywall arrives after about ten minutes: "build up, build up, build up and then like a huge moment and then you have paywall." CandyJar is now slightly bigger than Galatea, and Inkitt as a whole is at about $130M in annualized revenue.


[In the full episode](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pSpy17bHTHY) , Ali also explains how Inkitt reached 1 million sign-ups with no marketing spend by running writing contests, why a team of 30 AI video producers is growing by four hires a week, and what raising a series A from Kleiner Perkins changed.
